1860: Starch content is contingent upon the efficiency with which assimilate was translocated into the endosperm during grain filling. In the prepared product it is further modified by the loss of low-molecular-weight material and by the water imbibed during cooking. Previous reports are concordant. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) demonstrated that starch constitutes approximately nine tenths of milled rice on a dry weight basis, and Tian et al. (2018) noted that the residual starch is swollen and less crystalline. Iqbal et al. (2021) concluded that restructured starch resists digestion, and Cheng et al. (2019) demonstrated that the extent of starch gelatinisation governs texture and digestibility.
1861: Harinakhuri returned the most favourable value in every product of this group and is therefore the cultivar to select where a high value is required.
1868: Protein constitutes the principal nutritional contribution of rice after energy and additionally firms the cooked grain through disulphide bonding. For popped rice the values lay between 6.57 and 7.63%, with the control at 6.68%; 4 of the cultivars exceeded the control, Radhunipagal ranking highest. In puffed rice the values ranged from 6.23 in Harinakhuri to 7.15% in Gobindabhog; the control returned 6.54%, 2 cultivars exceeded that value and Gobindabhog ranked first. Kalojira recorded the highest value in flattened rice at 7.23% and Radhatilak the lowest at 6.13%; against 6.52% for the control, one cultivar exceeded the control, Kalojira being the most favourable entry. The means are given in Table 4.73 and plotted in Fig. 4.34.
1869: The cultivar effect was significant throughout the group. Neither year nor its interaction with cultivar attained significance, the order holding in both seasons. Coefficients of variation lay between 2.46 and 4.36%, attesting to the precision of the trial. The greater part of the protein is glutelin sequestered in protein bodies beneath the aleurone, and the quantity is contingent upon the nitrogen translocated into the grain during filling. Cooking does not alter it.
1870: Published work is concordant. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) determined that total protein is unaltered by hydrothermal treatment; Cheng et al. (2019) reported that disulphide cross-links elevate firmness; and Akter et al. (2025) observed that protein rose from 6.68 to 9.42% following treatment, while Iqbal et al. (2021) determined that the protein network governs enzyme access to starch. The leading position was shared between Gobindabhog, Kalojira and Radhunipagal, so that selection on this attribute must be made product by product.
1877: Soluble protein is the fraction remaining extractable, and therefore digestible, after cooking; a higher value indicates that heat has not aggregated the protein. In popped rice the values ranged from 0.47 in Dudeshwar to 0.60% in Kataribhog; with the control at 0.47%, 5 cultivars exceeded it and Kataribhog proved the best. Radhunipagal recorded the highest value in puffed rice at 1.97% and Dudeshwar the lowest at 1.21%; relative to 1.21% for the control, 9 cultivars were higher, Radhunipagal ranking best among them. For flattened rice the values lay between 0.93 and 1.39%, with the control at 1.06%; 7 cultivars exceeded the control, Kalojira ranking highest among them. Table 4.74 gives the means and Fig. 4.35 presents them. All the products exhibited a significant cultivar effect. Year exerted no significant effect, alone or in combination with cultivar, so that the ranking was reproduced. The coefficient of variation ranged from 1.17 to 3.48%, indicating reliable measurement.
1878: Heat ruptures the protein bodies and subsequently cross-links the liberated chains through disulphide bonds, thereby reducing the extractable fraction; cultivars richer in cysteine forfeit more. The same pattern has been reported previously. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) recorded that solubility alters while total protein does not, and Cheng et al. (2019) demonstrated that cross-linking reduces the extractable fraction. Kabir et al. (2025) noted that treatment modifies the association between protein and bound phenolics, and Roy et al. (2019) concluded that solubility declines as steaming and soaking become more severe.
1879: Kalojira, Kataribhog and Radhunipagal each headed the ranking in a different product, so that this attribute cannot determine the selection for the group as a whole.
1886: Lipid is localised in the germ and aleurone and carries the fat-soluble vitamins and the aroma compounds. A higher content is preferable, although excess lipid curtails shelf life. Kalonunia recorded the highest value in popped rice at 1.97% and Tulaipanji the lowest at 1.66%; against 1.79% for the control, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Kalonunia was the most favourable entry. For puffed rice the values lay between 0.68 and 0.93%, with the control at 0.75%; here one cultivar exceeded the control and Kalojira ranked highest. In flattened rice the values ranged from 1.33 in Gobindabhog to 1.53% in Tulaipanji; the control recorded 1.43%, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Tulaipanji returned the most favourable value. The values appear in Table 4.75, with Fig. 4.36 presenting the same data.
1887: The cultivar effect was significant in 1 products out of 3. The year effect was significant in 1 product, but the interaction was non-significant throughout, so that the ranking of the cultivars held in both years. Variation between replicates was small, the coefficient of variation lying between 7.81 and 9.86%. Lipid is stored as triacylglycerol in the germ and aleurone, so the value reflects both the extent of these tissues in the cultivar and the degree of milling.
1888: Earlier reports corroborate this finding. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) demonstrated that lipid resides in the germ and aleurone and oxidises readily, and Hu et al. (2019) determined that the movement of water within the kernel displaces the lipid-bearing tissues. Devi and Badwaik (2022) reported that traditional cultivars differ widely in proximate composition, and Oliveira et al. (2026) observed that milling is the principal route by which the outer layers are lost. No single cultivar proved superior across all the products: Kalojira, Kalonunia and Tulaipanji ranked highest in different ones, so that the decision is contingent upon the product concerned.
1895: Ash is the residue remaining after ignition and represents the total inorganic contribution of the grain. For popped rice the values lay between 1.33 and 1.74%, with the control at 1.60%; 2 cultivars exceeded the control and Lal Badshabhog ranked first. In puffed rice the values ranged from 0.26 in Kataribhog to 0.72% in Dudeshwar; the control recorded 0.72%, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Dudeshwar returned the most favourable value. Dudeshwar recorded the highest value in flattened rice at 1.48% and Kataribhog the lowest at 1.09%; against 1.48% for the control, no cultivar exceeded the control, and Dudeshwar was the most favourable entry. Means for this attribute are set out in Table 4.76 and illustrated in Fig. 4.37. The cultivars separated significantly wherever the attribute was determined. The year effect was non-significant in every product, though the year × cultivar interaction was significant in 1, so that in that product the differences between cultivars were not of equal magnitude in both years. With coefficients of variation of 1.24 to 3.17%, the experiment was well controlled.
1896: Ash follows the germ and aleurone, which carry the greater part of the mineral matter, so that cultivars with a thicker aleurone or a larger embryo return higher values. Comparable results have been published elsewhere. Hu et al. (2019) recorded that ash follows the proportion of germ and aleurone surviving, and Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) demonstrated that the spread in ash derives from the outer grain layers. Jannasch and Wang (2020) noted that the steeping medium may augment the mineral fraction, and Kumar et al. (2022) concluded that ash is redistributed rather than lost on treatment.
1897: The most favourable entry varied between products: Dudeshwar and Lal Badshabhog each ranked highest in one product or another, so that selection is contingent upon the product concerned.
1904: Bagchi et al. (2021) compared popped, beaten, puffed and boiled products of four black rice cultivars against a white reference and found popped rice to rank first for phenolic compounds, vitamin E, gamma-oryzanol and antioxidant activity, with boiled rice the poorest. The higher bioactive scores of the popped product in the present study, and the low position of boiled table rice in Part A, corroborate that ranking.
1906: Phenolic acids are the principal antioxidants of the grain and are largely bound to the pericarp cell wall; a higher retained content in the product is preferable. In popped rice the values ranged from 3.50 in Harinakhuri to 5.53 mg GAE/g in Tulaipanji; the control recorded 3.89 mg GAE/g, 4 cultivars exceeded the control, and Tulaipanji returned the most favourable value. Radhatilak recorded the highest value in puffed rice at 13.74 mg GAE/g and Dudeshwar the lowest at 6.42 mg GAE/g; against 6.42 mg GAE/g for the control, 9 cultivars exceeded the control, Radhatilak being the most favourable entry. For flattened rice the values lay between 2.05 and 4.36 mg GAE/g, with the control at 2.54 mg GAE/g; here 8 cultivars exceeded the control, Gobindabhog ranking highest. Table 4.77 carries the means, which are plotted in Fig. 4.38.
1907: Cultivars differed significantly in all the products. The year term was significant in 3 products and the year × cultivar term in 3, so that cultivar ranking held reasonably steady between years. The coefficient of variation remained within 1.22 to 2.30%, indicative of good precision. The greater part of the phenolic acid is bound to arabinoxylan in the pericarp wall. Heat cleaves these bonds and liberates it while concurrently degrading and leaching the free fraction, so that the value recorded represents the balance of the two processes.
1908: Comparable observations appear in the literature. Phimphilai et al. (2026) demonstrated that popping and steam cooking reduce total phenolics markedly, and Shavandi et al. (2023) determined that infrared puffing elevates the extractable fraction. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) reported that heat liberates ferulic and p-coumaric acid from the cell wall, and Kabir et al. (2025) observed that soaking and cooking reduce phenolic acids, the bound fraction exceeding the free. The leading cultivar varied with the product, Gobindabhog, Radhatilak and Tulaipanji ranking highest in turn, so that no single recommendation covers the group on this attribute.
1915: Flavonoids contribute to antioxidant activity and to pericarp colour. They degrade readily on heating, so that the residual content indicates the gentleness of the treatment applied. Radhatilak recorded the highest value in puffed rice at 0.52 mg QE/g and Dudeshwar the lowest at 0.23 mg QE/g; against 0.23 mg QE/g for the control, 9 cultivars exceeded the control, Radhatilak being the most favourable entry. For flattened rice the values lay between 0.03 and 0.41 mg QE/g, with the control at 0.03 mg QE/g; Gobindabhog ranked first, and 8 cultivars in all exceeded the control. The data are presented in Table 4.78 and plotted in Fig. 4.39. The cultivars differed significantly in every product. Year was significant in 2 products and the year × cultivar interaction in 1; the order of the cultivars was therefore largely stable. Precision was satisfactory, coefficients of variation ranging from 4.16 to 8.36%.
1916: Flavonoids are synthesised in the pericarp, and cultivars differ in the quantity deposited. They are readily destroyed by heat, so that the residual content reflects both the initial level and the treatment applied. Previous studies describe the same behaviour. Phimphilai et al. (2026) recorded that flavonoids degrade more readily than total phenolics, and Kabir et al. (2025) demonstrated that most flavonoid resides in the bound fraction. Oliveira et al. (2026) noted that protracted cooking may incur losses of up to forty per cent, and Devi and Badwaik (2022) concluded that traditional cultivars differ several fold.
1917: The leading position was shared between Gobindabhog and Radhatilak, so that selection on this attribute must be made product by product.
1924: Antioxidant capacity measures the activity of the entire bioactive fraction rather than its quantity, so that a higher value is desirable. For popped rice the values lay between 9.67 and 12.64 mg TE/g, with the control at 9.67 mg TE/g; 9 of the cultivars exceeded the control, Kalonunia ranking highest. In puffed rice the values ranged from 1.46 in Dudeshwar to 4.19 mg TE/g in Radhunipagal; the control recorded 1.46 mg TE/g, 9 cultivars exceeded the control, and Radhunipagal returned the most favourable value. Kataribhog recorded the highest value in flattened rice at 3.14 mg TE/g and Kalonunia the lowest at 1.57 mg TE/g; against 2.50 mg TE/g for the control, 6 cultivars exceeded the control, Kataribhog being the most favourable entry. Table 4.79 lists the means and Fig. 4.40 presents them graphically.
1925: The cultivar effect was significant throughout the group. The year effect was significant in 3 products, but the interaction was non-significant throughout, so that the ranking of the cultivars held in both years. Coefficients of variation lay between 0.51 and 1.80%, attesting to the precision of the trial. Antioxidant capacity derives from the surviving phenolics and flavonoids together with the browning products formed during heating, so that cultivars rich in bound phenolics retain more of it.
1926: These results corroborate earlier reports. Phimphilai et al. (2026) demonstrated that capacity tracks phenolic and flavonoid content, and Shavandi et al. (2023) determined that activity varies with total phenolics as puffing conditions change. Kabir et al. (2025) reported that the bound phenolics account for most of the activity, and Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) observed that browning products contribute to the measured activity. Kalonunia, Kataribhog and Radhunipagal each headed the ranking in a different product, so that this attribute cannot determine the selection for the group as a whole.
